title: The number that doesn't tie
text: Reconciling the quarter, a figure sits eleven thousand dollars off. It is a very clean error, the kind that doesn't happen by accident.

outcomes.text: It was a mistyped invoice by a junior. Easy fix, and I taught her the checks. She sent a card.
It led to a supplier who'd been double-billing for years. The firm recovered the money. I was noticed.
He went pale, said he'd handle it, and the matter vanished. I thought about it often.
He thanked me. A month later he was gone.

choices.label: Plug the gap and move on

outcomes.text: I made an adjusting entry. It balanced, and it bothered me for months.
An auditor found it a year later. I explained, and it cost me.

title: Tax week
text: Fourteen clients, one deadline and a shared printer that jams on the third page. A client has dropped off a shoebox of receipts and said, 'Everything's in there.'

choices.label: Go through the box line by line

outcomes.text: I found a legitimate deduction he'd never have claimed. He tipped me in whisky.
The box was mostly napkins. I did what I could.

choices.label: Ask him to resubmit it sorted

outcomes.text: He did. It saved me an evening.
He fumed and took his business elsewhere.
It passed. Nobody was happier or sadder.
The tax office queried it. I spent a month on letters.

title: The campaign that nobody asked for
text: Your pitch is two hours from presentation. The client wants 'edgy but safe', 'viral but classic'. The last slide has your best joke on it, and your boss hates it.

outcomes.text: The client laughed out loud. The campaign won an award.
The client didn't get it. The room was horribly quiet.
The deck was safe and forgettable. It was approved without a flicker of feeling.
The client said it lacked 'spark'. I wanted the floor to open.
They picked the joke. My boss pretended it was his idea.
They picked the safe one, then asked about the joke for a month.

title: The post that went wrong
text: A cheerful social post you scheduled lands at the same moment as a sad news story. Within an hour it is being quoted back at the brand, with screenshots.

outcomes.text: A short, sincere apology. The internet moved on in a day.
The apology was screenshotted too. A long weekend.
The storm passed. Nobody ever fired anyone.
The silence was louder than the post. The client was furious.
Self-deprecating, quick, and perfectly pitched. It turned the mood.
It landed badly. A newspaper picked it up.

title: The model says no
text: Your forecast shows the product line the CEO loves will lose money for three years. He has already announced it.

outcomes.text: He listened, and for once did not shoot the messenger. The product was re-scoped.
He thanked me coldly. I was moved to another team within a month.
It looked better. It was all my fault when the real numbers came in.
Nobody checked. Nobody ever checks. I didn't sleep.

choices.label: Show it privately to someone who can act

outcomes.text: The CFO took it quietly and turned the ship. I was thanked in private.
It leaked. The CEO found out. He didn't forgive me.

title: The beautiful dataset
text: A messy dataset hides a pattern that nobody has seen: customers who buy on Tuesday are twice as likely to churn.

outcomes.text: It led to a big discovery and a real change in strategy. I got a promotion track.
It was a statistical fluke. I felt a bit silly, but I learned.
The team ran with it. I got a credit in the deck.
Someone else presented it. I stayed quiet and furious.
I verified it for months. Eventually it came out right.
A competitor published it first.

title: The load test
text: The bridge model passes every test but one, and the one it fails is a rare combination of wind and traffic that probably never happens.

outcomes.text: It cost two weeks and delayed the deadline. The design was better for it.
The client balked at the cost. I was backed by the senior engineer.
Cheap and elegant. Nobody even noticed.
It was too elegant: it hid the real issue.
It stood for fifty years. Nobody ever knew.
A storm tested it. It held, barely. I aged ten years in a night.

title: The prototype
text: Your prototype works, which is the problem. Management wants to ship it Monday. It has never run for more than six hours.

outcomes.text: They gave me a week. I found three failures. The product was safer.
They gave me one day. It wasn't enough, but it was something.
It worked. Nobody read the warning.
A customer was injured. I replayed it for years.
A bit of rule-bending that no one ever knew about. Good engineering.
It broke the schedule and my reputation took a hit.

title: The client's cousin
text: The client's cousin, an amateur, 'just has a few suggestions' that would turn your elegant atrium into a glass-fronted car park.

outcomes.text: The cousin was flattered to be heard. The atrium survived.
The cousin escalated to the client. A very long lunch.
It was awful. I showed him why. He conceded.
It was surprisingly not awful. I borrowed one idea.
It was built. It was ugly. It won no prizes.
It was built, and the cousin took all the credit. I did the paperwork.

title: The last model night
text: The competition deadline is at nine in the morning. The model is balsa, glue and exhaustion, and at 3 a.m. a corner collapses.

outcomes.text: I rebuilt it by dawn, bleary and proud. It placed second.
It came out better. It won.
I called it 'a ruin by design'. The jury loved it.
The jury did not.
I slept for 12 hours and felt fine.
I regretted it for years.

title: Make the logo bigger
text: The client's feedback on version nine: 'Can you make the logo bigger? Also smaller. Also more minimal.' The deadline is Thursday.

choices.label: Do all three and send options

outcomes.text: They picked option two, which was my favourite anyway.
They picked all three and told me to combine them.
They listened. The final was elegant, and they thought it was their idea.
They threatened to go elsewhere. They bluffed.
It looked like a billboard. They loved it.
It looked terrible. They loved it anyway.

title: A stolen idea
text: Scrolling through a competitor's site, you stop dead: your layout, your palette, your odd little rounded-corner trick. It's a pixel-perfect match.

outcomes.text: They took it down and apologised. I felt dignified.
They ignored it. A lawyer would cost more than the job.
It trended. They were embarrassed. A few clients came to me out of sympathy.
It trended against me. I looked petty.
I did. It stung, and then it didn't.
I was hurt for a long while, and then I made something better.

title: The source who won't go on record
text: A person in a position to know calls you at midnight with a story that could end a career. 'But I'll deny I said it,' they say.

outcomes.text: It took three weeks and two more sources. The story ran, and it was true.
I couldn't confirm it. We killed the story. I felt the loss for months.

choices.label: Run it with the one source

outcomes.text: It ran. It was true. It was luck, nothing more.
It was wrong. The retraction was humiliating.
Someone else ran it a week later. I watched with envy.
The story never came out. Sometimes that's the way.

title: The doorstep
text: A tragedy has hit the town, and your editor wants a quote from the family of the victim. You stand at their door with a notebook that feels like a weapon.

outcomes.text: The mother let me in. We sat in the kitchen for two hours. I didn't use a word of it until she asked me to.
They shut the door, gently. I wrote about that instead.
They called a week later. A quiet, dignified piece.
They never called. I ran the piece without them.
I got it. I hated myself for it.
The father shouted at me. I deserved it.

title: The silence
text: A teenager sits in your office for the third session and says nothing. At minute forty-five he mutters, 'You'd just tell my mum.'

outcomes.text: I laid out what I could and couldn't keep private. He thought about it, and began to talk.
He listened, nodded and left. He never came back.
He opened up. Then I learned something I couldn't keep to myself. I had to break it.
It worked. It also felt like a lie I'd have to pay for.
We sat for another ten minutes. At the end he said, 'Same time next week?'
The silence was just silence. But he came back.

title: A client in a good mood
text: A long-term client announces that she is doing so well she'd like to stop. You are not sure, but she is certain.

outcomes.text: A graduation of sorts. We marked it with a handshake. She wrote a year later: fine.
She relapsed within a month. I felt I'd failed her.
We ended slowly. It worked.
She was cross. She came back anyway.
She stayed. I kept her dependent, and I knew it.
She left, offended. A fair reaction.

title: The contaminated plate
text: Six weeks of cell culture ruined by a single fuzzy spot in the corner. The professor is coming for his Monday update.

outcomes.text: He grunted and said 'it happens'. He ordered a restart. I loved him a little for it.
He sighed, and lost his temper, then apologised. Awkward.
He bought it. It was later found to be faulty, to my relief.
The facilities team checked the incubator and found nothing. I was caught.
I caught up in four weeks. He never knew.
He noticed the date mismatch. I explained, and it went fine.

title: An odd result
text: A routine sample comes back showing something that shouldn't be there at all. Not a mistake, you think. Not a mistake.

outcomes.text: She went very quiet and then very excited. It became a paper, and my name was in the acknowledgements.
She dismissed it. A year later someone else published it.
It repeated. The odd result was real.
It didn't repeat. A relief, and a letdown.
I will never know what that was.
It haunted me every time I saw that sample number.

title: Inspection day
text: An environmental health officer arrives unannounced at the lunch rush and starts opening fridge doors with a torch. In the third is last Tuesday's stock.

outcomes.text: She noted it and moved on. We got a four-star rating. The staff cheered.
She wrote it up and we got a two. The owner was furious.
A tour of the pastry section did it. Deeply unprofessional, deeply effective.
She saw right through me. A fine followed.
She took the blame. We didn't speak after.
The sous chef quit. So did half the team.

title: The critic's table
text: The waiter whispers: the woman at table six is writing the review that will make or break the season. Her fish has just come back with a request for 'a little less salt'.

outcomes.text: She cleaned the plate. Her review used the word 'precise'.
She sent the second one back too. Four stars, 'a stumble'.

choices.label: Send it back with a smile

outcomes.text: She noticed the cheek and loved it.
She found it condescending. The review stung.
I stormed into the walk-in. I was fine. The fish was fine.
I yelled at the commis. I regret it.

title: Recital night
text: Your most talented student freezes on stage. Fifty parents hold their breath. Fourteen bars of nothing.

choices.label: Walk on and sit beside her

outcomes.text: I played the left hand, gently. She found her place. The room clapped for a long time.
She cried, but she finished. I held her afterwards.
She breathed, and started again. Perfect.
She never played again. A hard one.
She found her way. It took a minute. She was stronger for it.
She walked off. Her parents were furious with me.

title: The prodigy
text: A new student, nine years old, sits down at the piano and plays a Bach prelude from memory, and then asks, 'Is that right?'

outcomes.text: She became my favourite student. I never felt prouder.
She outgrew me in a year. I passed her to a conservatoire, proud and a little hollow.
A hard thing to do, and the right one.
She never forgave her parents for moving her.
I held her back. I know it.
She quit music at fifteen. I'll never know why.

title: The missing exhibit
text: At 11 p.m. the night before the hearing, you notice exhibit F is missing from the bundle, and exhibit F is the whole case.

outcomes.text: She cursed, laughed, and drove in. We rebuilt it by dawn.
She was furious. We found it in a different folder. I almost cried.
I found it at 3 a.m. under a coffee ring. I didn't tell anyone how close it was.
It was gone. I recreated it from emails and prayer.
The judge noticed. I was named in court.
No one did. I'll never be that lucky again.

title: A client in the corridor
text: A man corners you in the corridor of the court and says, quietly, 'I didn't do it. Please tell them.' You're not supposed to talk to him at all.

outcomes.text: He listened. It changed his cross-examination. The client was acquitted.
He said it was irrelevant. The client was convicted.
The case went as it went. I think about him sometimes.
He looked at me like I'd forgotten a promise.

choices.label: Tell him to speak to his lawyer

outcomes.text: Correct, professional, and a little cold.
He nodded, hollow-eyed, and did.

title: A missed check-in
text: A young man on your caseload hasn't turned up for two appointments. Breaching him is the rule. His mother has just called, in tears.

outcomes.text: He'd lost his job and was ashamed. We put a plan together. He kept every meeting after that.
He was drunk and angry. I stayed calm. It was a long hour.
By the book. The court sent him back to prison. His mother never forgave me.
He was taken. A year later he told me it saved him.
He took it, and didn't waste it.
He wasted it. My supervisor reminded me about the rules.

title: The good news
text: A woman you've supervised for three years walks in with a job offer letter, shaking, holding it out like it might break.

outcomes.text: We both laughed, then cried a little. A day I'll remember.
She went and told her kids. I closed the office and cried, privately.
I shook her hand. She'd have liked more, but she understood.
I regretted it for a long while.
A sensible step. It was a good place.
It wasn't. I got her out before she signed.

title: Form 27-B
text: A citizen has filled in Form 27-B, but the box that needs ticking only exists on Form 27-C. Both forms have been withdrawn.

choices.label: Bend the rule and tick it

outcomes.text: The citizen's problem went away. Mine began a week later in a staff meeting.
It was a small kindness that slipped through. I'll never know if it mattered.
It took six weeks. The citizen wrote a thank-you note and I cried.
The supervisor found a loophole in an hour. I felt silly.
A regrettable day. The queue grew.
The citizen wept. I felt it for a week.

title: The reorganisation
text: A memo arrives announcing a 'transformation programme'. Your department will be 'streamlined' by Christmas. Nobody will say what that means.

outcomes.text: I joined the team and shaped the plan. My job was safe, and it was the right call.
I became the face of the cuts. I was not liked.
I found a better role at another department. I left on good terms.
The market was dry. I stayed, uneasy.
My role survived. Half my floor didn't.
I was moved to a job I hated.

title: The settlement offer
text: The other side has offered a settlement. It's good, but not great. Your client wants to take it. You think you can win.

outcomes.text: A safe, reasonable resolution. The client wept with relief.
I regretted it when I saw the verdict in a similar case, a month later.
We won, handsomely. The client was thrilled, and I felt invincible.
We lost. The client lost everything. I live with that.
They took the offer. It was their right. I stood by them.
They went to trial. It was their right. It went wrong.

title: The inconvenient email
text: While preparing disclosure, you find an email from your own client that could sink his case. The rules say it must be disclosed.

outcomes.text: The client was furious, then relieved. Honesty won the judge, and the case.
We lost, and the client fired me. My name is clean.
He did. The matter settled quietly.
He refused, and I withdrew from the case.
It came out at trial. I was reported to the regulator.
No one ever found it. I know it's there, in a box.

title: Bad news at 5 p.m.
text: A test result has come back, and it's the kind you'd never wish on a person. The patient is in the waiting room, smiling at her phone.

outcomes.text: I sat down and said it plainly and kindly. She was quiet, then asked three good questions. I felt I'd done it right.
She cried in the room and thanked me. It took a long time to go home.

choices.label: Ask her to come back tomorrow

outcomes.text: A restless night for both of us, but it gave me time to plan the conversation.
She read it online first. I'll never forgive myself.
It was handled kindly. It was not mine to handle, and I knew it.
My colleague did it badly. The patient complained.

title: The 3 a.m. page
text: You've been awake for twenty-two hours when the page goes. A young man in the ER with a fever and a rash that you've only read about.

outcomes.text: It was meningitis, caught in time. He walked out a week later. I slept for a day.
It was nothing; a rash from a new detergent. An expensive night, but safe.
He got worse. We caught up, barely.
He got better. Judgment calls are the job.

choices.label: Ask a colleague for a second look

outcomes.text: She saw it in a second. I swallowed my pride.
She was asleep. I woke her. She was gracious, and right.

title: The terrified patient
text: A grown man has gripped the arms of the chair so hard his knuckles are white. He needs a root canal, and he has not had a check-up in fifteen years.

outcomes.text: He relaxed gradually. Afterwards he said it was 'not that bad'. He booked a check-up.
He gasped at every sound. We finished. He wrote a nice review.
A safe, sleepy hour. He was grateful, and chatty afterwards.
It worked too well. He said some funny things about his mother.
It was fast. He vowed never to return.
He fainted. We laughed about it later.

title: The upsell
text: The practice manager hands you a target: whitening packages, up 20% this quarter. A patient with perfectly good teeth sits waiting.

outcomes.text: I told her to save her money. She thanked me and referred three friends.
The manager frowned. The patient came back anyway.
She bought it. It looked nice. I felt cheap.
She sensed it. She didn't return.
She agreed. A fair compromise.
She declined. We parted friends.

title: The prescription that looks wrong
text: A dose on a prescription is ten times what it should be. The doctor's number goes to voicemail and the patient is shifting from foot to foot.

choices.label: Refuse to dispense and keep trying the doctor

outcomes.text: I reached her after twenty minutes. A misplaced decimal. She thanked me, and meant it.
The patient was furious about the wait. It didn't matter. It was right.
It was right. I'd misread it. I felt dumb.
It wasn't right. A patient was hospitalised.
It worked, and nobody was harmed. It was against the rules.
It didn't treat the illness. The patient returned in a worse state.

title: The regular who asks too much
text: An older man asks about his tablets for the fourth time this month. You realise he isn't confused, he is lonely.

outcomes.text: We talked about his garden. He bought a small thing for his cough, and left lighter.
He kept me twenty minutes. The queue grew. He apologised and I said it was fine.
I answered. I didn't forget his face.
He stopped coming. I wondered about that.
He joined a choir. He came in to tell me.
He politely refused. I left it there.

title: The choice no one wants
text: A family brings in a fourteen-year-old dog, failing fast. The cost of treatment is huge, the outlook poor. The children are in the corner, silent.

outcomes.text: We said goodbye together. The kids sat on the floor with her. I cried in the car.
They chose treatment. She had three more good months.
They spent everything they had. It worked, for a while.
It didn't work. They were bankrupted and bitter.
A gentle ending. They thanked me, quietly.
They went elsewhere. The dog died there a week later.

title: Farm call at dawn
text: A farmer rings at five: a mare in labour for three hours with no progress. The road is ice. You pull on your boots in the dark.

outcomes.text: A breech foal. It took an hour. Both lived. The farmer made me tea and I could have wept.
The mare died. The foal lived. I had to hand-feed it for a week.
It sorted itself. A lucky pass.
It went wrong. I should have gone.
She went and did well. I envied her for it.
She was out of her depth. I drove out after.

title: The board wants blood
text: The quarter is bad, the board is restless, and the chair has suggested 'efficiencies'. A list of four hundred names is on your desk.

choices.label: Cut the list in half and cut your own pay

outcomes.text: The board grumbled. The staff noticed. Morale, remarkably, held.
It wasn't enough. The next quarter I cut the rest.
Cold, quick, defensible. I couldn't look at the car park for a month.
A newspaper got hold of the list. I was the villain.
I proposed a pay cut across the board. It was a bold move and it worked.
The board replaced me. I was out in a month.

title: The offer from the rival
text: A rival's CEO takes you to dinner. Across the tablecloth he slides a figure: 40% more, and a bigger title. 'You're wasted where you are.'

outcomes.text: A new chapter. I took my best people with me and felt like a pirate.
The new firm was a mess. I'd made a mistake.
My own board matched it in a day. A bit humiliating, a lot profitable.
They called my bluff. I had to take it.
Loyalty paid off. Within a year I was promoted.
A year later he was my boss. Awkward.

title: The peer review
text: Reviewer Two has written a savage critique of your paper, which includes the line 'The authors appear unaware of the literature'. They are quoting a paper they have written.

outcomes.text: The editor sided with me. The paper was published.
It took a year. The paper came out, but I aged.
It felt wonderful. I deleted it before sending.
I sent it. The editor remembered it for a decade.
They became my biggest supporter. Academia is petty and generous.
They didn't notice. I did.

title: The student who wants a letter
text: A student who has missed half your lectures asks for a letter of recommendation for a funded programme. 'I'm just more of an independent learner,' he says.

outcomes.text: He was shocked, and a little ashamed. He came to the next lecture.
He complained to the dean. The dean backed me.
He got in. He worked harder than he ever had.
The programme wrote back asking questions. I was careful.
He got in, and wasted it.
He got in, and called me from there. He'd changed.

title: The result that breaks the model
text: Your data contradicts the theory your whole group has spent a decade building. The professor wants a clean paper by spring.

outcomes.text: It was controversial, then confirmed. A career-defining moment.
It cost me my funding and my mentor. I still believe it was right.
Same result. A restful certainty.
A different result. I'd made a mistake; a relief and a shame.
The paper sailed through. I hated the paper.
A reviewer asked about the missing data. I was found out.

title: Observation time
text: A rare slot on the telescope opens: eight hours of sky, after a three-year wait. The weather forecast says clouds.

outcomes.text: A clear patch opened at midnight. The data was gorgeous.
Clouds all night. I stood outside and just looked up.
She got her data. I got a favour owed.
Her night was clear. Mine would have been.
The next slot was a year away.
It rained. I was relieved.

title: The forced march
text: Thirty kilometres in full kit, in rain, on four hours' sleep. At kilometre twenty-two the soldier next to you says, quietly, 'I can't.'

outcomes.text: We both made it. He's been my friend ever since.
I hit the wall at twenty-eight. We crossed the line together, limping.
He gritted his teeth and finished. He thanked me, wordlessly.
He dropped out. He took it hard.
I finished well. He did not. I thought about it.
He was picked up by the truck. I was awarded something I didn't want.

title: The order that feels wrong
text: Your sergeant gives an order that violates the written rules of engagement, quietly and with confidence. Everyone else is already moving.

outcomes.text: It cost me a promotion. A year later, an inquiry vindicated me.
The sergeant yelled. The lieutenant changed the order.
I wrote the report. It went nowhere. I didn't forget.
Nothing happened. That's not the point.
I did what I was told. I live with it.
It was fine. I'll never know if that's lucky or terrible.

title: Heavy weather
text: Day nine of a storm at sea. The deck moves like a living thing. A rope has parted and a crate is sliding toward a sailor at the rail.

outcomes.text: I held it long enough for him to clear. I broke two ribs.
It missed him by a hair. I was told off for the risk.
He ducked. The crate hit the rail and splintered.
He didn't hear me.
A team arrived in thirty seconds. Everybody was fine.
It took too long. Someone was injured.

title: Shore leave
text: Port at last, after seven weeks at sea. A free evening, the town's neon on the water, and a message from home that you haven't answered.

outcomes.text: It was the best hour of the trip. They told me I sounded like myself.
The call was bad news. I sat on the dock a long time.
A loud, warm, brilliant night. I remember maybe half of it.
A fight started and I got involved. I spent the next day on report.
Eleven hours. The best investment of the trip.
I woke up with the world's worst crick in my neck.

title: The pre-flight check
text: A tech has signed off an aircraft, but a gauge you glance at on the walk-round isn't reading right. The brief is in ten minutes and the schedule is tight.

outcomes.text: It had a fault that would have killed someone. I got a quiet commendation.
It was a loose connection. The squadron lost an hour and I lost some patience.
It held. A very long flight.
It failed in the air. I got down by the skin of my teeth.
The tech found it. We both learned something.
He was offended. It took a month to smooth over.

title: The long deployment
text: Eight months away. In the last video call, your kid held up a drawing and said, 'This is you,' and it was a stick figure on a screen.

outcomes.text: The letters became a book on the family shelf.
The mail was slow, but it arrived. They kept every one.
Efficient, hollow, effective. I came home a stranger.
I was promoted. My family wasn't impressed.
They approved it. I was home for the birthday.
They refused. I made peace with it.

title: A warning light at cruise
text: At thirty-eight thousand feet, an amber light blinks on. The co-pilot says 'sensor?' in the voice of a man hoping to be right.

outcomes.text: A faulty sensor, as we'd hoped. We landed on time. The passengers never knew.
A real fault, minor. We diverted. Everyone cheered when we touched down.
It cleared. I felt an old man's relief.
It didn't clear. I was lucky.
Fire trucks lined the runway. It was nothing. The airline was grateful I'd erred on the side of caution.
Fire trucks lined the runway. It was nothing. The airline was less grateful.

title: Fog at the destination
text: The destination is closed in fog, the alternate is an hour away, and fuel is adequate but not generous. The passengers don't know.

outcomes.text: The sensible, boring choice. We landed with a comfortable margin.
The airline wasn't pleased. Safety isn't cheap.

choices.label: Hold and wait for a gap

outcomes.text: The fog lifted. We landed. I let out a breath I'd held for an hour.
It didn't lift. We had to divert with less fuel than I liked.
A low, beautiful, nerve-shredding landing. Passengers applauded.
Missed approach. A go-around. My heart took a week to settle.
